S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any battery-related fire, thermal runaway, injury, evacuation, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it. Other confirmed thermal incidents must be reported within 5 business days.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-accepted protocol and representative production units. A model with a failure rate above 5% must promptly submit a regulator-approved corrective-action plan, including interim risk controls and a retest schedule.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed systems must support a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with clear customer instructions and safeguards against unauthorized activation. For systems already installed, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent upgrade plan and complete implementation within 6 years of this standard taking effect.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New battery systems manufactured for sale must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard takes effect. The suppression system must be designed and validated for the battery’s chemistry and enclosure, and maintained according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide the underlying model-specific data and a corrective-action plan. The regulator must promptly investigate and determine appropriate protective measures, including recall where warranted by verified incident data, severity, trends, exposure, and corrective actions.

document.section_notes: S1 is broadly acceptable: serious reports within 24 hours, other confirmed incidents within 5 business days, and customer notice within 5 business days. S2 keeps the 55 °C test and 5% benchmark but permits above-limit sales under an open-ended corrective-action plan, so it is weakened despite customer-level numeric disclosure and no public publication. S3 and S4 land in acceptable ranges with a 6-year retrofit deadline and 36-month suppression deadline; S5 is weakened because the 8-per-100,000 threshold triggers notification and corrective action, not mandatory recall, leaving recall to regulator discretion.
